--- Page 1 ---
Dissecting the Carbon–SLO Tension in
Geo-Distributed LLM Serving
Burak Topcu, Musa Cim, Zuhal Ozturk, Mahmut Taylan Kandemir
Department of Computer Science and Engineering
The Pennsylvania State University
State College, PA 16801, USA
{bvt5283, mtc5693, zbo5031, mtk2}@psu.edu
Abstract—Large Language Model (LLM) inference is driving a
growing share of datacenter carbon emissions. Although carbon-
aware scheduling can reduce these emissions in geo-distributed
datacenters by exploiting the spatiotemporal variations in grid
carbon intensity, the latency-sensitive nature of LLM serving
constrains this design space. While prior studies investigate
the carbon savings achievable through spatial scheduling, they
oversimplify the dynamics of modern inference engines, such as
queueing and continuous batching, which strongly shape inference
latency. We address this issue by designing and evaluating a
latency-centric, geo-distributed inference simulator, calibrated
with hardware-grounded latency and power measurements, that
reproduces these dynamics and enables the study of carbon
savings under strict service-level objectives (SLOs). We then
formulate a series of SLO- and carbon-aware schedulers of
increasing sophistication, from per-request heuristics to batch-
level optimization: (i) a greedy heuristic, (ii) an integer linear
programming (ILP)-based scheduler jointly assigning batches of
requests, (iii) an iterative ILP-based solution projecting its own
assignments back into the load estimates to capture load coupling,
and (iv) a facility mixed-integer linear programming (MILP)
scheduler pricing the energy of batched requests collectively
rather than in isolation. Across three LLMs under MLPerf SLOs
and varying system loads, the MILP-based option offers the best
carbon–SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions by up to 60%
relative to the round-robin policy, with an average SLO violation
of 3%. Our characterization further shows that savings grow
with the spread of carbon intensity across datacenters and shrink
as system load increases, while SLO attainment depends on how
frequently schedulers receive datacenters’ load updates.
Index Terms—Geo-distributed LLM Services, Carbon-Aware
Inference Scheduling, LLM Inference.
I. INTRODUCTION
Over the past decade, LLM-powered applications have
become widespread across domains [1]–[3], driven by break-
throughs in reasoning [4], [5] and agentic pipelines [6]–
[8], turning inference into a continuously running workload
worldwide. Sustaining this inference demand has spurred
massive investments in accelerator-rich datacenters [9]–[11]
and raised concerns about their environmental impacts [12],
[13]. The International Energy Agency projects the energy use
of accelerator-equipped servers to grow by 30% annually, over
three times faster than conventional ones, and to reach nearly
half of net datacenter energy use through 2030 [14]. Beyond
energy consumption, this growth directly translates into carbon
emissions through the carbon intensity (hereafter, CI) of the
grids powering these sites, increasing their share of the overall
carbon chain [15]. Recent studies [16], [17] show that inference
already emits over 25× more carbon than training throughout
a model’s lifetime, underscoring the need for carbon-efficient
inference serving.
Despite the adoption of green energy-based solutions [18],
[19], renewable availability varies temporally and spatially [20],
[21], limiting their capacity to address inference-related
emissions. Complementing these strategies, prior work has
traded either output quality or serving performance for carbon
reduction. The former selects the carbon-optimal LLM that
meets an accuracy target [22], [23] or shortens outputs through
prompt-level directives [24]. The latter preserves output quality
while trading latency for lower emissions, either by reducing
energy use or by scheduling inference to greener datacenters.
As energy efficiency has been studied across the compute stack
for decades [25]–[27], recent efforts exploit the remaining slack
through frequency scaling under latency service-level objectives
(SLOs) [28], [29] or load-adaptive inference configurations [30].
However, carbon savings with these energy-oriented approaches
diminish as the load increases, limiting their effectiveness at
scale. In contrast, CI varies by more than an order of magnitude
across regions and over time [31], offering significant potential
to reduce inference-related emissions through carbon-aware
scheduling while preserving output quality.
Temporal scheduling that suspends and resumes jobs based
on green energy availability [20] is appropriate for delay-
tolerant workloads but not for latency-critical ones, such as
LLM inference with stringent time-to-first-token (TTFT) and
time-per-output-token (TPOT) objectives. Spatial scheduling
can meet latency constraints, subject to data-placement regu-
lations such as GDPR [32], but suffers from load imbalance,
as carbon-greedy policies dispatch requests to the greenest
datacenters and inflate per-token latency. While carbon-aware
spatiotemporal scheduling has been studied for batch ML
training, HPC [33]–[35], and even for latency-sensitive web
services [36], [37], only a small but growing body of work
explores its spatial axis for LLM inference across geo-
distributed datacenters.
Table I summarizes studies that aim to reduce inference-
related emissions by scheduling requests across datacenters
using linear or integer programs [39], [40], metaheuristics [38],
or learning-based search [41], [42]. Unfortunately, these studies
overlook several key facets of real-world inference scenarios:

(i) most [38]–[40], [42] schedule requests to datacenters at
coarse time intervals and assume load-independent latency,
which hinders capturing how TTFT and TPOT change in
practice as continuous batching [44] dynamically admits and
completes requests; (ii) none fully models power as a function
of inference workload and phase, although prefill and decode
exhibit distinct compute utilization [45], driven by the prefill
length and the batch size, respectively; (iii) none accounts for
the queueing delay when an inference engine lacks memory for
a new request, and some [40], [43] further ignore inter-region
transfer delays; and (iv) their latency targets are mostly self-
defined rather than grounded in standard benchmarks such as
MLPerf [46]. Consequently, these studies oversimplify practical
latency and power dynamics and lack representative evaluation
against benchmark-grounded per-token SLOs, limiting their
applicability to real-world deployments.
To study carbon-aware LLM scheduling under real-
world serving conditions, we develop a latency-centric, geo-
distributed serving simulator.1 It instantiates datacenters across
multiple regions, each with GPU-equipped nodes hosting
configurable data-parallel inference engines and forwards
requests between regions [38], [40], [42] over measured
inter-region network latencies [47]. Engines capture iterative
continuous batching behavior [44], model queueing delays by
admitting requests only when sufficient memory is available,
and estimate per-inference phase latency and power using
analytical models calibrated across different models, degrees
of parallelism, and datasets. Using this simulator, we further
design and test a suite of carbon-aware schedulers, from a
lightweight carbon-weighted greedy policy to integer programs,
and characterize their trade-offs among carbon, SLO attainment,
and tail latency against both carbon-blind and carbon-aware
baselines [39], [43]. Our novelty lies in identifying the engine-
level datacenter state, namely the active batch load and queue
depth, from which a carbon-aware scheduler can estimate TTFT
and TPOT at scheduling time, which, to our knowledge, no
prior carbon-aware geo-distributed scheduler has explored. Our
main contributions are as follows:
• High-fidelity simulator: An extensible simulation frame-
work for geo-distributed LLM serving, validated end-to-end
within a node against real inference, that captures inter-
region transfers and key serving features, such as continuous
batching and engine queueing, using calibrated per-phase
latency and power models over configurable topologies and
1https://github.com/topcuburak/carbon-slo-at-geoscale
scheduling policies.
• SLO- and carbon-aware schedulers: A series of schedulers
of increasing sophistication, from per-request heuristics to
batch-level optimization:
– Greedy: minimizes a weighted carbon-latency score per
request at negligible overhead.
– Standard integer linear program (ILP): jointly assigns
batches of requests, treating each datacenter’s load as fixed
during the assignment.
– Iterative ILP: re-projects datacenter batch states after each
ILP solve to capture load coupling and re-solves until the
assignment converges or an iteration limit is reached.
– Facility mixed-integer linear program (MILP): models
batched energy as a shared per-datacenter cost and a
marginal per-request cost, discouraging the scattering of a
batch across many datacenters.
• Carbon–SLO frontier characterization: A comprehensive
evaluation of carbon savings and SLO attainment across
models, prompt lengths, system loads, and CI variation
against carbon-blind and carbon-aware baselines. The facility
MILP achieves the best carbon–SLO balance, reducing
carbon emissions by up to 60% relative to the round-robin
policy with an average SLO violation of 3%, whereas
the most carbon-aggressive greedy setting, at comparable
savings, violates the SLO for up to 55% of requests. We
further analyze the TTFT tail behavior, scheduling overhead,
sensitivity to load-update frequency, topology, robustness to
facility overheads, and predicted output lengths.
II. BACKGROUND
Carbon intensity (CI) and carbon accounting. Electricity
grids are supplied by a mix of sources G, each with a distinct CI
in gCO2/kWh. The grid’s overall CI is a generation-weighted
average CI = P
g∈G(Pg/Ptotal) · CIg, where Pg and CIg denote
the power contribution and intensity of source g, and Ptotal
is the total grid power. Low-carbon sources such as nuclear
and solar have median CIs below 50, whereas fossil sources
such as natural gas and coal have medians of 490 and 820,
respectively [48]. Fluctuating renewable availability and power
demand on grids over time change the energy-source mix,
leading to a spatially and temporally varying CI.
The Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol [49] is an inter-
national standard for measuring, managing, and reporting
greenhouse gas emissions from operations, value chains, and
mitigation actions. It defines three emission scopes, with
2


--- Page 3 ---
emissions from powering datacenters (hereafter, DCs) used
for LLM inference falling under Scope 2, also referred to as
operational emissions [50]. CI signals are sampled at fixed
intervals (e.g., hourly), and the operational emissions of a
DC over K intervals are quantified as PK
k=1 Etot[k] · CI[k],
where Etot[k] = Ptot[k] · ∆t is the total energy consumption
in the interval k while operating with a total average power
Ptot[k]. The DC power is Ptot = PIT × PUE, where power
usage effectiveness (PUE) accounts for facility overheads such
as cooling and lighting.
Geo-distributed LLM serving. Online (i.e., server) or in-
teractive LLM inference scenarios [46] are evaluated under
per-token latency objectives: TTFT, which covers queueing
and prefill durations, and TPOT, which corresponds to the
average time for output token generation [51]. Both latency
metrics depend on the engine’s load and its serving features. For
example, continuous batching [44] can admit new requests at
each iteration, shortening queueing and hence TTFT; however,
each admitted prefill intervenes in the ongoing decode pipeline
and extends the TPOT of active requests. Chunked prefill [52]
and disaggregated serving [45], [51] mitigate this by splitting
prefills across steps or running prefill and decode on separate
resources, offering control over the TTFT–TPOT balance.
To meet these latency SLOs under varying system loads
at scale, deployments place data-parallel replicas of tuned
inference engines across geo-distributed DCs [53], [54] and
coordinate them through centralized [55], decentralized [56],
or hierarchical [57] control planes. However, as highlighted
in [36], [57], centralized designs are inherently vulnerable
to a single point of failure and to bottlenecks under high
loads, since each decision passes through the central scheduler,
whereas decentralized designs lack a consistent global view and
incur significant coordination overhead. Therefore, we adopt a
hierarchical design, as in several other studies [36], [58], in
which a global provisioner maintains a consistent view of DC
states, and regional schedulers either place requests on a local
DC or forward them to a peer scheduler for inference serving.
III. GEO-DISTRIBUTED LLM SERVING MODEL
This section formalizes the geo-distributed LLM serving
problem, introduces our hardware-calibrated latency and power
models, and presents our simulator, which builds on these
models and emulates inference features such as iterative
continuous batching.
A. Problem Formulation
We model the geo-distributed LLM serving setup with a
set of regional schedulers S and a set of DCs D, where each
scheduler s ∈S manages a subset of D, and each DC d ∈D
comprises identical nodes, each with a host and multiple GPUs
configured as inference engines. A request r = (tarr
r , pr, SLOr)
arrives at its nearest scheduler s at time tarr
r
with a prompt pr
and per-token SLOr defined by the service provider for the
serving model. The scheduler either dispatches r to a local DC
d or forwards it to another scheduler s′, which dispatches it
to a remote DC d′. At the target DC, an inter-node scheduler
assigns r to a node, whose host selects an inference engine
through an intra-node policy, and r waits in that engine’s queue.
Once admitted for inference, r undergoes a prefill and a series
of decode steps until the end-of-sequence (EOS) token, within a
batch of other ongoing requests. Despite identical data-parallel
inference engines, heterogeneous prompt lengths and dynamic
arrivals inherently lead to a load imbalance among them [59].
Given a request stream R, regional schedulers dispatch
requests to DCs to meet their per-token SLOs while minimizing
operational carbon emissions. The total emissions across
DCs are CO2 = P
d∈D Ed · CId, where CId is DC d’s grid
CI during the serving window. The energy consumption of
a DC accumulates over its nodes, each comprising a host
and inference engines, as Ed = PUEd · P
t Pd(t) · δt, where t
indexes simulation steps of length δt. The DC power is
Pd(t) = P
n∈d
␀P host + P
e∈n P eng
e
(t)
, where P host and P eng
e
(t)
are the host and engine e powers of node n in DC d,
respectively. Since all compute resources within a DC share
the same power source and facility infrastructure, we model
each DC with a single PUE and CI [36], [41]. We detail the
per-inference step latency and power model (i.e., P host and
P eng) under varying loads in Section III-B and the inference
engine’s processing behavior in Section III-C.
Our hierarchical design decouples scheduling decisions from
per-DC state collection via a central provisioner, which polls
DCs every ∆p seconds for i) active batch size Bd, ii) engine
queue depth in tokens Qd, iii) KV-cache occupancy KVd,
and iv) prefill duty dutyd (i.e., the recent fraction of time
spent in prefill), each averaged over the DC’s engines, together
with the DC’s grid CI, CId. It broadcasts these as a global
snapshot to all schedulers, along with the inter-region latency
matrix RTT(s, s′). We intentionally use per-DC averages since
statistics at per-node or per-engine granularity would enlarge
the polling payload and the schedulers’ decision cost.
B. Inference Latency and Power Modeling
LLM inference proceeds in two phases: prefill processes
all input tokens in one forward pass, and decode generates
one token per step autoregressively. Both phases pass requests
through a stack of mostly identical transformer blocks, whose
kernel dimensions are determined by the model architecture,
parallelism strategy, and per-step workload [60]. Even in
mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, which activate experts
unevenly, kernels with fixed dimensions (e.g., GEMMs) repeat
across blocks and dominate per-step latency [61]. As inference
phases execute the same-dimension blocks sequentially (e.g.,
32 times for Llama-3.1-8B), we model prefill and decode step
latencies analytically and compose these models with engine-
level mechanisms, such as memory constraints and continuous
batching, to simulate end-to-end inference.
Prefill Latency. Figure 1-a plots prefill time across input
tokens for Llama-3.1-8B [62] and Qwen2.5-7B [63] at two
tensor-parallel degrees (TP=1 and TP=2), and for Mixtral-
8x7B [64] at TP=4. Prefill latency stays nearly flat up to a
few hundred tokens (e.g., 400 for Mixtral-8x7B at TP=4),
where GPU compute is not yet saturated, and then grows
3


--- Page 4 ---
Fig. 1. Per-engine latency model across models and TP degrees: (a, b) prefill and decode step time across prefill lengths and batch sizes, respectively; (c)
prediction error against measured step time, with per-setup MAPE.
approximately linearly with the total prefill length. Therefore,
for a given model, parallelism strategy, and hardware, prefill
latency can be expressed as a function of the total prefill length.
We model it as tpre = ttok(N) + b0 + b1B + b2
P
i n2
i, where b0
and b1B are the fixed per-step cost and per-request overhead for
B requests, and b2
P
i n2
i is the quadratic attention cost across
prompt lengths ni. The token term ttok(N), which captures
the cost of processing a total of N tokens, is piecewise linear
in N, with its slope increasing after the saturation point k.
We calibrate these coefficients and saturation points separately
for each inference setup, using vLLM v0.6.3 measurements in
FP16 on A100 GPUs with prompts from diverse datasets [65]–
[67] spanning 32 to 32K tokens. The model predicts prefill step
time within 1.7% MAPE for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B
across both TP degrees, and within 4.8% for Mixtral-8x7B at
TP=4 (Figure 1-c), whose prompt-dependent expert activations
vary the execution time for the same token count.
Decode Latency. Unlike prefill, decode steps generate one
token per request by reading model weights and the KV
cache, making decode memory-bound [45]. Batching amortizes
each step’s weight read across requests, but GPU memory
bounds the batch size as KV caches grow. As Figure 1-b
shows, decode step time grows sublinearly with batch size B,
as larger kernels improve compute utilization [60], but rises
sharply after saturation. It further increases with the cached
context because each step reads the KV cache for all batched
requests. We capture both trends with a low-order polynomial
that is quadratic in B, tdec = a0 + a1B + a2B2, where each
coefficient varies linearly with the mean cached length per
request ℓ= K/B as aj = αj + βjℓand K is the total number
of cached tokens. We calibrate the coefficients using the same
inference measurements as in prefill, spanning batch sizes and
KV-cache occupancies close to each setup’s memory limit. Our
model predicts decode step time within 3.4% MAPE across all
five setups (Figure 1-c), but since decode steps typically take
tens of milliseconds, transient thermal and frequency effects
become more visible and limit this accuracy.
Power Model. In addition to the latencies, capturing the
dynamic power dissipation during inference is necessary for
carbon accounting. Figure 2 shows the measured average
per-GPU power across the prefill and decode steps for the
same setups. Prefill power starts below the TDP (400 W for
A100 [68]) for the shortest prompts but quickly reaches it
once the tokens saturate compute resources, consistent with
Figure 1-a. Decode power, instead, grows sublinearly with
Fig. 2. Per-GPU power during (a) prefill and (b) decode across models and
TP degrees.
batch size and reaches about 95% of TDP for larger batches,
with a slight drop at the largest batch sizes. With higher degrees
of parallelism, e.g., TP=2 for Llama, the transformer kernels
are sharded across GPUs, so per-GPU power starts at a lower
value and reaches the TDP at larger input workloads.
We model the energy of each inference step as the av-
erage power times the step latency. A prefill step costs
Epre = epre
0
+ epN + ea
P
i n2
i, where epre
0
is the prefill fixed
step energy, epN is the compute energy of N prefill tokens,
and ea
P
i n2
i is the marginal attention energy capturing the
effect of the prompt lengths ni. Similarly, a decode step costs
Edec = edec
0
+ edB + ekK, where edec
0
is the fixed decode step
energy, edB is the compute energy of B batched requests, and
ekK captures the energy of reading the K cached tokens. The
power model, calibrated per inference setup on the campaigns
shown in Figure 2, predicts held-out step energy within 5.6%
MAPE across all setups. Additionally, the simulator accounts
for two standing costs: i) when a model is loaded and ready to
serve but no request is in flight (i.e., the idle state), an engine
draws about 72 W per A100 GPU, and ii) each node incurs
a nearly constant host power P host, which we set to 300 W,
as the CPU package alone draws about 146 W under engine
load on our testbed, and the remainder covers host memory,
networking, and peripherals.
C. Geo-distributed LLM Inference Simulator
Our simulator, depicted in Figure 3 on an illustrative
deployment, consists of four major components communicating
over gRPC: (i) a load generator, (ii) regional schedulers, (iii)
DCs, and (iv) a provisioner. The load generator, represented in
the figure by requests (e.g., Req-1 and Req-2), emits prompts
from a dataset and dispatches them to the schedulers 1 at
a configurable Poisson rate λ, emulating real-world demand
with varying prompt lengths and stochastic arrivals.
4


--- Page 5 ---
A regional scheduler (e.g., US-South) schedules each request
on a local or remote DC using a policy described in Section IV.
When the policy selects a remote DC, the scheduler forwards
the request to the target region’s scheduler 2 , incurring an
inter-region transfer delay, and the remote scheduler admits
the request into its scheduling window before placing it on
the target DC 3 . Scheduling policies can optimize a single
objective or several at once, such as carbon and latency. Any
such policy needs objective-specific state from the DCs. For
the carbon–latency trade-off, we design the simulator such
that each node continuously maintains per-engine counters for
active batch size, queue depth, KV-cache occupancy, and prefill
duty. In every polling period ∆p, the provisioner pulls these
counters averaged over each DC’s engines, along with the grid
CI of the DC 4 , and broadcasts them to all schedulers with
the inter-region latency matrix 5 . Schedulers consume these
to optimize latency and carbon objectives together through
distinct policies. We analyze the impact of the polling period
on scheduling quality in Section V-C.
Fig. 3. Overview of the simulator architecture on an example topology.
At the target DC, the inter-node scheduler assigns the request
to a node, and the intra-node scheduler dispatches it to an
inference engine, where it joins the engine’s queue (e.g., Q#1
in Figure 3). Each engine emulates a continuous-batching loop
in wall-clock time, with a configurable maximum batch size
similar to vLLM’s max_num_seqs [69], and a model-specific
constant KV cache size per token (e.g., 128 KiB for Llama-3.1-
8B), determining how many tokens fit into the engine memory
left after the model weights. At each inference step, the engine
first retires finished requests and then admits queued ones
as long as the batch size with the new request stays within
its batch limit and the new request’s KV cache fits into its
remaining memory. Hence, the queueing delay depends on the
engine’s occupancy rather than being a fixed constant.
Admitted requests can be processed in several prefill steps,
depending on the input sequence length (ISL). For example, a
prompt whose ISL exceeds the per-step token budget, similar
to vLLM’s max_num_batched_tokens [69], is split across
consecutive steps, each lasting tpre and stalling the ongoing
decode batch. The updated batch then advances by one decode
step lasting tdec, recomputed for the current batch and KV
cache size, so that admissions and completions change the
inference step time at every iteration. Engines sleep for
each predicted step duration, so latencies accumulate in wall-
clock time. A request’s TTFT thus includes the scheduling
delay, any inter-region transfer, queueing time, and prefill
duration, whereas its TPOT is the average of the decode step
latencies, including those stalled by other requests’ prefills.
Alongside latency, engines accumulate energy throughout
inference, charging Epre per prefill step, Edec per decode step,
and idle energy when there are no requests in the inference
pipeline. Together, the simulator reproduces the latency and
energy dynamics of modern inference engines, such as vLLM,
which we validate within a node deployment in Section V-B.
IV. CARBON-AWARE SCHEDULER DESIGNS
Building on the simulator’s calibrated inference latency
and energy models, we investigate the carbon–SLO trade-off
through a series of scheduling policies of increasing sophisti-
cation, from per-request heuristics to batch-level optimization:
(i) a per-request greedy heuristic, (ii) a standard batch-based
integer linear program (ILP), (iii) a load-coupled iterative ILP,
and (iv) a facility-location mixed-integer linear program (MILP)
that prices the energy of batched requests collectively. All
four schedulers share a common latency estimator to predict
TTFT and TPOT for each request-DC pair (r, d) using the
analytical step models given in Section III-B. The estimated
TTFT is TTFTr,d = RTT(s, s′) + Wd + tpre(ISLr + Qd), where
RTT(s, s′) is the inter-region transfer delay (zero for a local
DC placement), Wd is r’s wait time for a batch slot at an engine
in d, and tpre(ISLr + Qd) is the prefill time of r together with
Qd previously queued prompt tokens. The estimated TPOT is
TPOTr,d =

tdec(Bd + 1, KVd) + T pre
d

/(1 −dutyd), where Bd
and KVd are the average batch size and KV occupancy per
engine in d, with +1 accounting for r joining the batch, the
factor 1/(1 −dutyd) for prefills already running at d, and T pre
d
for those still queued, amortized over r’s output length. Both
latency estimates rely on inputs available at scheduling time:
ISLr from tokenizing r’s prompt, and Bd, Qd, KVd, dutyd,
and RTT(s, s′) from the provisioner’s latest snapshot.
The TPOT (only in T pre
d
) and carbon estimates require
r’s output sequence length (OSL), which is unknown until
inference ends. For example, a request with an OSL of 100
occupies an engine roughly 10× longer than one with an OSL
of 10 and consumes proportionally more decode energy, so an
approximate OSL matters for placement quality. We evaluate
the schedulers with both oracle and predicted OSLs, where
the latter is the median quantile estimated by a lightweight
two-layer MLP (detailed in Section V-C) from the request’s
ISL, serving model, and application type. With these estimates,
the scheduler compares the predicted TTFT and TPOT with
the serving model’s budgets to identify SLO-feasible DCs.
The following four policies then trade carbon against latency
among the feasible DCs, differing in their cost models, how
they project load onto DCs, and the granularity at which they
schedule requests.
A. Carbon-Aware Greedy Scheduling
The greedy policy makes an independent scheduling decision
for each request using a scoring function. For an incoming
request r, the scheduler first filters out DCs that violate the
5


--- Page 6 ---
per-token SLOs via the analytical TTFT and TPOT estimates,
and then scores the remaining SLO-feasible DCs, Fr, with:
scorer,d = α
Latr,d
maxd′∈Fr Latr,d′ + (1 −α)
CId
maxd′∈Fr CId′
(1)
where Latr,d = TTFTr,d + OSLr · TPOTr,d is the estimated
end-to-end latency of r at d, and r is dispatched to the
lowest-scoring DC. The trade-off parameter α ∈[0, 1] weighs
latency against carbon, with α=1 prioritizing latency and α=0
prioritizing carbon. The key weakness of the greedy policy is
that it scores each request in isolation and cannot coordinate
placements across requests. Thus, within a polling period, it
keeps dispatching requests to the same carbon-latency optimal
DC until the projected load drives that DC to the SLO boundary.
Since the regional schedulers operate concurrently on the same
snapshot, their combined dispatches easily push the DC beyond
this boundary, violating request SLOs.
B. Carbon-Aware Batch Scheduling via ILP
In contrast to greedy per-request scheduling, the batch
schedulers aggregate requests over a short window ∆w or
up to a fixed count and jointly assign them by solving an ILP,
which limits the load placed on any DC and removes herding
among a scheduler’s own requests. Let R denote the requests
accumulated in ∆w, and let xr,d ∈{0, 1} indicate whether r
is assigned to d ∈Fr, where Fr is the SLO-feasible DC set
for r. The assignment is obtained by solving:
min
x
X
r∈R
X
d∈Fr

(2a)

X

xr,d = 1,

xr,d ≤Hd,
∀d ∈D
(2c)
where cr,d = PUEd · Er,d · CId is the carbon cost of serving r at
d, and Er,d is the energy consumed for serving r at d under the
power model of Section III-B (i.e., the increase in step energy
from its prefill and its OSLr decode steps). Hd = max(0, capd−
loadd) represents the remaining slots in d’s total batch capacity
capd (i.e., the per-engine batch capacity times its engine count),
with loadd corresponding to active and pending requests in the
projected view of d. Since each xr,d appears in one assignment
equality and one capacity inequality, the constraint matrix is
totally unimodular, and the LP relaxation yields integral optima.
We solve the ILP as a linear program with HiGHS [70] within
tens of milliseconds.
The standard ILP solves this program once per window,
estimating each request’s feasibility against the same pre-
window state without accounting for the other requests placed
in the window. Hence, a DC feasible for each request alone may
violate SLOs once they are placed together, as their combined
batch and queue push TTFT and TPOT beyond the estimates.
To address this load-coupling gap, we formulate the iterative
ILP, which feeds each solution back into the view. After each
iteration t, the assignments n(t)
d
= P
r x(t)
r,d are projected onto
each DC’s batch size and queue as if already dispatched, and
TTFT(t)
r,d and TPOT(t)
r,d are recomputed with the updated states
to refresh F(t)
r
and E(t)
r,d. Equation (2) is then re-solved until
two consecutive iterations yield the same assignment or Tmax
rounds elapse, at the cost of several solves per window.
C. Carbon-Aware Batch Scheduling via MILP
However, the ILP-based schedulers account for interactions
among requests assigned to the same DC only through capacity
and latency constraints while treating their carbon costs
independently, as in prior per-request formulations [39], [43].
Consequently, they estimate the carbon cost of serving multiple
requests as the sum of their individual costs, overlooking the
shared energy consumption of batched inference. In practice,
requests within the same batch share an inference engine’s
energy, including a fixed per-step energy cost that does not
scale with batch size. For example, when two requests are
assigned to an idle engine, an additive model charges the
engine’s activation cost twice, even though both requests can
share a single batch and incur that cost only once.
To address this, we formulate a facility MILP that separates
the fixed carbon a DC pays once if it serves any request in
the window from the per-request cost cr,d. It adds P
d fd yd
to the objective in Equation (2a) and replaces the capacity
constraint in Equation (2c) with P
r xr,d ≤Hd yd, where
yd ∈{0, 1} indicates whether d receives any requests from
the window, and fd is the carbon of waking d’s engines. With
this capacitated facility MILP, the wake-up cost is charged
once per DC, regardless of how many requests are placed
there. Although harder to solve than the ILP, the MILP adds
only |D| binaries (i.e., one yd per DC) compared with the
|R| · |D| assignment variables, so HiGHS solves it within the
0.25 s time limit. We evaluate the carbon–SLO trade-offs of
all four schedulers, together with their scheduling overheads,
in Section V-C.
V. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
A. Experiment Setup
Geo-distributed setup. We evaluate our schedulers across four
regions (EU-North, US-East, Asia, and South America), each
with four DCs (e.g., Netherlands, Belgium, Lithuania, and
Latvia for EU-North) whose CI is drawn from Electricity
Maps [31]. Each DC comprises four nodes of 8×A100-
40GB GPUs [68], and its hourly CI (i.e., the finest available
granularity) is held constant within a run. The inter-region
transfer delay is the measured one-year p50 RTT between
the corresponding AWS regions [47]. We use a uniform PUE
of 1.1 [71] by default and assess real-world sensitivity with
per-DC PUE values from public disclosures [72]. As three
DCs lack public PUE data, the PUE, CI, and topology studies
replace them and their CIs with the nearest-CI sites in each
region. Within DCs, both inter-node and intra-node schedulers
use round-robin so that the measured carbon savings stem
solely from the regional schedulers’ decisions.
Simulator configuration. We evaluate the proposed schedulers
on geo-distributed deployments of Llama-3.1-8B at TP=1 and
Mixtral-8x7B at TP=4, for which the MLPerf Inference Server

both oracle and predicted
scenario [73] sets (TTFT, TPOT) SLOs of (2 s, 100 ms) on
CNN-DailyMail [74] and (2 s, 200 ms) on its OpenOrca-based
workload [75], respectively. Since MLPerf evaluations typically
run on a single node, we relax both TTFT budgets to 3 s to
account for inter-region forwarding, scheduling, and inter-node
dispatch delays, while keeping the TPOT budgets unchanged.
We further evaluate Qwen2.5-7B [63] under the Llama-3.1-8B
trace and SLOs to test whether our findings generalize beyond
the MLPerf models. The load generator emits requests with
Poisson arrivals at the rates in Table II and dispatches them
round-robin to the four schedulers for 200 s per policy-rate pair
on a single 64-core server, allowing engines to reach a stable
load within the first 15 s, leaving over 90% of each run at
steady-state occupancy. We define the load regime by the ratio
of the mean per-engine batch size under round-robin to the
batch capacity: i) below 15% as low, ii) 15–40% as moderate,
and iii) above 40% as high load. Accordingly, we use 1200,
2400, and 4000 req/s as the low, moderate, and high loads
for the 7B and 8B models, and 800, 1200, and 2000 req/s for
Mixtral-8x7B.
Scheduler configuration. We sweep the greedy policy over the
α values in Table II, from carbon-only (α=0) to latency-leaning
(α=0.9). Both ILP- and MILP-based policies batch requests
over a 100 ms window that closes early at 300 requests, with
at most Tmax=3 iterations for the iterative ILP and a 0.25 s
solver limit for the MILP. When a solver fails or cannot place a
request within capacity, the scheduler falls back to the lowest-
carbon SLO-feasible DC with headroom (i.e., greedy with
α=0), and to round-robin (RR) if none exists. We use oracle
OSLs in all experiments except the OSL sensitivity study.
As carbon-blind baselines, we test RR and least-loaded (LL),
which schedule each request individually. We further compare
our schedulers against Green-LLM [39], with its hourly per-DC
token budget mapped to the engine batch limit, and MOER-
based routing [43], porting only their scheduling decisions
into our system. MOER-based routing sends each request to
the lowest-CI SLO-feasible DC, and thus coincides with our
greedy policy at α=0.
Evaluation metrics. Our primary metrics are total operational
carbon in gCO2, including idle and host energy, and per-
token SLO violation, defined as the fraction of requests that
miss either their TTFT or TPOT budget. Carbon savings are
measured against RR at the same load. Since SLO violation
rates hide tail latency, we additionally analyze the p50, p90, and
p99 TTFT across policies, as well as the per-request scheduling
overhead.
B. Simulator End-to-End Validation
Beyond the per-step analytical models in Section III-B, we
validate the simulator against real end-to-end inference serving.
We deploy three data-parallel Llama-3.1-8B vLLM engines (the
same version as in calibration) at TP=1 on A100-40GB GPUs
and dispatch CNN-DailyMail prompts to them with the RR
policy at Poisson arrival rates from 2 to 50 req/s. The rates span
7% to 181% of the engines’ measured capacity (27.58 req/s
under saturation), covering both the queue-free and queueing
regimes. We then replay each run through the simulator with
all decisions fixed, sending every request to the same engine
at its logged arrival time with its logged ISL and actual OSL,
so that the comparison isolates the engine model.
Across the 19 rates and over 40K requests, the simulator
captures the TPOT latencies that vary from 15.5 ms to 54 ms
as prefills increasingly stall decode steps, with an average error
of less than 5%. It further reproduces TTFT latencies, ranging
from 71 ms to over 20 s as queueing builds up, with an overall
average error of 9.1%, which varies from 3.5% below saturation
and 5.2% under overload to 28.5% around saturation, where it
conservatively overestimates TTFT. Running a single engine
instead of three of them at the same per-engine load changes
TPOT by only 3.3%, confirming that co-located engines do not
interfere with each other and can be modeled independently.
In addition, the simulated GPU energy stays within 2.5% of
the measurement at all arrival rates, showing that the simulator
closely captures the end-to-end engine behavior from queue-
free operation to overload.
C. Carbon–SLO Characterization
Figure 4 presents the carbon–SLO trade-off across scheduling
policies at moderate and high loads, including SLO violations
against normalized carbon savings relative to RR and TTFT tail
behavior at high load across all models. We omit the low-load
case from the figure, where all carbon-aware schedulers except
greedy at α=0 and Green-LLM [39] remain within 1.3% SLO
violation, and the facility MILP achieves the highest carbon
savings across all models (53.8–59.6%).
Carbon–SLO violation trade-offs. As Figure 4a shows, the
greedy policies exhibit α-monotonicity, with savings rising and
SLO violations growing as α decreases. At moderate system
loads, greedy at α=0 (equivalent to MOER [43]) achieves
7


--- Page 8 ---
(a) Carbon saving relative to RR and SLO violation for each policy.
(b) TTFT tail behavior per policy at high load, from p50 to p99 with ticks at
p50/p90. Labels show carbon savings relative to RR.
Fig. 4.
Carbon–SLO trade-off and TTFT tail behavior across scheduling
policies, loads, and models. G denotes greedy policies, with α=0 corresponding
to the MOER [43] policy.
carbon savings similar to those of the ILP- and MILP-based
policies but violates the SLO for up to 6.9% of the requests on
the dense models and 44.8% on Mixtral-8x7B. This is because
it concentrates the load on the greenest DCs without a capacity
limit. Conversely, greedy at α=0.9 saves at most 3% carbon
with negligible SLO violation. The ILPs, the facility MILP,
and greedy at α=0.5 perform similarly on the dense models,
achieving up to 54% carbon savings within 1.9% violation,
whereas Green-LLM [39] reaches comparable savings with up
to 7.2% violation, as its batch-agnostic latency estimates never
reject a loaded DC. On Mixtral-8x7B, however, the facility
MILP stands out, saving up to 8.6 percentage points more than
these policies at a 1.3% SLO violation.
At high system loads, the highest savings shrink to 32–38%
as the green DCs saturate. Greedy at α=0 saves 7.3 percentage
points more than α=0.5 on average, but incurs 12.1 points
more violations, with the gap widening from Qwen2.5-7B to
Llama-3.1-8B to Mixtral-8x7B. This ordering follows each
model’s per-step decode latency (Figure 1-b), which leaves
progressively less TPOT headroom under the RR policy (from
71% to 51% of the budget), and concentrating the load on
greener DCs thus results in more SLO violations. Furthermore,
greedy at α=0.9 emits more carbon than RR on the dense
models, as its latency term redirects requests from the loaded
green DCs to dirtier ones. In contrast, the standard ILP and the
facility MILP remain robust owing to their per-window capacity
constraints, saving up to 32.8% on dense models and 35.0%
on Mixtral-8x7B, with SLO violation rates of up to 12.5%
and 2.4%, respectively. Green-LLM saves about 5 percentage
points more on dense models but substantially worsens SLO
violations (up to 30.7%), and on Mixtral-8x7B, it saves 7.6
percentage points less than the facility MILP, with a violation
rate of 25.6%.
Tail latency across policies. Since the SLO violation rate
hides the severity of violations, we break down the TTFT tail
behaviors at high system loads, where queueing pressure is
most severe, in Figure 4b. On the dense models, the greedy
policies achieve the lowest median TTFT (i.e., p50) among
the carbon-aware schedulers (around 0.5 s), as they place each
request upon arrival without a batch capacity constraint. The
standard ILP and the facility MILP raise the median up to 1.2 s,
mostly because their capacity constraints cluster arrivals at the
DCs, doubling the prompts fused per prefill step, on top of the
solver overhead. The iterative ILP raises the median to 1.8 s
due to repeated solves, while Green-LLM reaches only 0.9 s
by avoiding clustered arrivals but keeping the green engines at
their batch limit, which increases the queueing wait. The p99
TTFT stays within the 3 s budget under the greedy policies,
but reaches up to 3.6 s with the standard ILP, the facility MILP,
and Green-LLM, and further climbs to 7.5 s with the iterative
ILP due to solver overheads. This indicates that greedy at
α=0 violates the SLOs through TPOT rather than TTFT, as it
concentrates decode batches on the greenest DCs.
In contrast, the Mixtral-8x7B setup at TP=4 runs a quarter
as many engines per DC as the dense models at TP=1 and
serves about three times longer outputs (a mean OSL of 211
compared to 71 tokens for Llama-3.1-8B). Greedy without a
batch capacity constraint thus quickly saturates the green DCs,
raising the median TTFT to 3.3 s at α=0 due to an average
queueing time of 2.9 s, whereas the ILP- and MILP-based
schedulers keep the median within 0.7 s and their queueing
time around 0.2 s. The p99 TTFT reaches up to 8.8 s with
the carbon-aggressive greedy policies (i.e., α≤0.5) and Green-
LLM but remains within 2.2 s under the ILP- and MILP-based
schedulers, showing that the capacity constraints enforced by
these policies matter most for the model with the smallest
TPOT headroom.
Fig. 5. Carbon saving and SLO violation at high load under uniform and
real per-DC PUE [72] (a). Facility MILP savings at the base hour and three
lowest- and highest-CV hours (CV of CI across DCs) from 2021 to 2024,
under varying loads (b).
PUE and CI Sensitivity. In practice, PUE varies across DCs
and CI varies across regions and over time, making carbon
savings sensitive to both. To analyze the sensitivity of our
findings to real per-DC PUE, we replace the uniform PUE of
1.1 with operator-reported per-DC values, ranging from 1.08
(e.g., Netherlands) to 1.32 (e.g., Japan), and evaluate the most
carbon-aggressive greedy, ILP, and MILP-based policies. As
Figure 5-a shows, real per-DC PUEs increase the savings of all
carbon-aware schedulers at high load, with the facility MILP
8


--- Page 9 ---
improving from 29.2% to 30.5% on Llama-3.1-8B and from
36.6% to 38.7% on Mixtral-8x7B. In the real PUE data, the
dirtiest grids have the highest PUE (e.g., the Japanese DCs
combine a CI of 449–502 gCO2/kWh with a PUE of 1.32),
which inflates the carbon of RR more than that of the carbon-
aware schedulers. However, their SLO violation remains nearly
unchanged, as expected, since PUE mainly rescales each DC’s
energy use rather than changing where requests are placed.
Furthermore, Figure 5-b shows how carbon savings respond
to the spatiotemporal variation of CI. To quantify this variation,
we compute the coefficient of variation (CV), i.e., the standard
deviation of CI divided by its mean, across DCs at each hour
in our CI data. Among the 35K hours from 2021 to 2024, we
select the three lowest- and highest-CV hours as well as the
base hour and test the facility MILP scheduler at those times.
From the lowest (CV of 0.31) to the highest-CV hour (CV of
0.94), carbon savings rise from 49/44% to 59/55% at low load,
from 34/39% to 56/55% at moderate load, and from 13/24%
to 39/45% at high load on Llama-3.1-8B/Mixtral-8x7B models,
while the SLO violation remains unchanged. Even though low
and moderate system loads leave more room for carbon savings
(as more engines in the green DCs remain underutilized), the
facility MILP still saves up to 39–45% carbon across models
at high load when the CI spread across DCs is large.
Fig. 6. Per-request scheduling time at high load, spanning p50 to p99 (a).
SLO violation at moderate load across polling periods, under synchronous
and asynchronous polling (b). Carbon saving and SLO violation when serving
Llama-3.1-8B at high load across various topologies (c).
Scheduler Overhead, Polling Period, and Topology Sensi-
tivity. As schedulers differ in decision granularity and solver
invocations, we compare their per-request scheduling overhead
at high load in Figure 6-a. The greedy policies decide in under
1 ms, while the standard ILP, the facility MILP, and Green-
LLM show similar overheads with a p99 of up to 0.5 s. The
iterative ILP incurs the highest overhead (a p99 of 6.5 s on
Llama-3.1-8B), as its repeated solves saturate the solver at
1000 req/s per scheduler. Overall, despite solving a mixed-
integer program, the facility MILP offers the best carbon–SLO
balance at a comparable overhead. Moreover, these schedulers
rely on the DC loads periodically broadcast by the provisioner,
so the freshness of this snapshot is critical. To investigate
how snapshot freshness affects SLO violation, we vary the
polling period under both synchronous and asynchronous
polling in Figure 6-b. With a polling period of up to 2 s,
the facility MILP keeps the SLO violation below 10% for
both models (at most 8.2%), but at 5 s, the violation rises
to 10.5–32%. Hence, the freshness of load feedback directly
bounds the SLO attainment in geo-distributed scheduling.
Furthermore, asynchronous polling offers no consistent benefit
over synchronous, as staggered polling only spreads the
snapshots over time without reducing their age.
Additionally, we study how topology design affects the
carbon–SLO trade-off. Beyond the base topology, we design
a topology with 8 schedulers, halving the DCs per scheduler,
and another with 4 schedulers that halves the total number of
DCs while doubling the nodes per DC, so that all topologies
have the same number of engines. As Figure 6-c shows for
the facility MILP on Llama-3.1-8B, doubling the schedulers
keeps the carbon savings almost unchanged but nearly doubles
the SLO violation (10.3% to 19.4%), as more schedulers
concurrently concentrate load on the same green DCs from
the same snapshot. In contrast, fewer but larger DCs reduce
the violation to 4.1% as DCs absorb more load, but lower the
savings to 23.2% since fewer green DCs remain to schedule
requests on.
Fig. 7. Carbon saving and SLO violation at high load with oracle and predicted
OSLs (a). Facility MILP on Mixtral-8x7B with long and mixed prompts as
the per-engine batch capacity grows in steps of 4 and 8, respectively (b).
OSL Prediction and Prompt Length Sensitivity. Since the
OSL of a request is unknown at scheduling time, we study
replacing the oracle OSL with the OSL estimate of a lightweight
predictor, following prior length-aware schedulers [76]. We
train a two-layer MLP (128 hidden units, about 27K parameters)
that takes the log ISL, the serving model, and the dataset (i.e.,
the application type) as inputs and runs in under 0.1 ms per
request. It jointly classifies each request into one of six OSL
buckets and estimates its OSL quantiles, and the scheduler uses
the median quantile as the OSL. Although only 51% (Llama-
3.1-8B) and 37% (Mixtral-8x7B) of the estimates fall into the
correct bucket (compared to 17% for a random guess), 99%
and 70% fall in the correct or an adjacent bucket. As Figure 7-a
shows, predicted OSLs barely move any scheduler, changing
carbon savings by at most 1.3 points on Llama-3.1-8B and
4.1 points on Mixtral-8x7B, and raising SLO violations by at
most 1.1 points, except for the iterative ILP on Llama-3.1-8B,
whose results vary with its decision latency.
We further evaluate sensitivity to prompt length, since the
MLPerf workloads have short-to-moderate ISLs (a mean of 841
tokens for CNN-DailyMail and 195 for OpenOrca). We use a
long set of prompts drawn from GovReport [67] and a mixed set
of prompts drawn from six datasets [65]–[67], [74], [75], [77]
with a mean ISL of 10.7K and 2.9K tokens, respectively, on
Mixtral-8x7B. Since longer prompts occupy more KV cache per
9


--- Page 10 ---
request, the batch capacity that an engine can sustain changes.
Thus, we sweep the per-engine batch capacity and relax the
TTFT budget to 4.5 s for both scenarios as long prompts reach
a p99 TTFT of 1.7 s even at low load under the RR policy. We
choose the rates (50 and 200 req/s) so that RR fills about 40%
of the per-engine KV cache, the moderate-to-high boundary
measured by KV occupancy. As Figure 7-b shows, the facility
MILP saves up to 30% carbon at a batch capacity of 16 on long
prompts and 28% at 24 on mixed prompts, while keeping the
SLO violation near 5%, indicating that carbon-aware scheduling
generalizes across context lengths.
VI. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS
Discussion. Our findings show a significant potential for carbon
reduction in geo-distributed LLM serving. We further observe
that schedulers leave some engines idle (i.e., ready to serve
but waiting for a request) while distributing requests across
DCs under varying loads. For example, with the facility MILP,
Llama-3.1-8B TP=1 engines remain idle for 73%, 56%, and
33% of the time at low, moderate, and high loads, respectively,
compared with at most 10% under the RR policy. Depending on
the load, the idle and host energy account for 28 to 81% of the
remaining carbon, over 85% of which comes from DCs with
above-median CI, motivating a load-aware engine activator that
adjusts the number of active engines to the demand. We further
studied tensor parallelism (TP), as it is commonly used to meet
aggressive latency targets [60]. With TP=2, each DC hosts half
as many Llama-3.1-8B engines, each using twice the GPUs
for the same batch with a sublinear speed-up, partly due to
inter-GPU communication. We observe that at high load, these
fewer engines saturate sooner, tightening the TPOT budget and
limiting load shifts toward green DCs, so the facility MILP
emits 22% more carbon with higher SLO violations, making
data-parallel deployment preferable.
Limitations. We validate the simulator within a single node
for Llama-3.1-8B only, since end-to-end data-parallel dispatch
requires several engines, whereas a single Mixtral-8x7B engine
at TP=4 already fills our four-GPU node. Our latency and power
models are calibrated on A100 GPUs, and other accelerators
would shift the absolute carbon and latency values, although
our carbon–SLO findings, driven by batching and queueing
dynamics, are expected to extend to them. Additionally, our
workloads consist of independent single-turn requests, so while
our long prompts stress the KV cache, multi-turn sessions,
where prefix caching couples consecutive requests to the DC
that holds their KV cache, are left for future work.
VII. RELATED WORK
Reducing the carbon footprint of computing has been
studied along two complementary axes. Embodied carbon from
hardware manufacturing is addressed through carbon-aware
hardware and DC design [50], [78]–[80], while operational
carbon, which depends on compute energy and grid CI, is
reduced by temporally shifting delay-tolerant workloads [20],
[81], spatially scheduling workloads across regions [34], [36],
or scaling resources with CI variation [35]. For LLM serving,
model-level techniques select the carbon-optimal model that
meets an accuracy target [22], and generation-level methods
shorten outputs via prompt directives [24], while system-level
approaches reconfigure cluster size, parallelism, and GPU
frequency to reduce energy consumption [30], [82].
As interactive LLM inference with stringent latency SLOs
is not amenable to temporal shifting, existing carbon-aware
LLM serving approaches exploit spatial CI variations across
DCs, as summarized in Table I. SLIT [38] and MARLIN [42]
schedule requests across DCs based on periodically forecasted
load, using a genetic algorithm and multi-agent learning,
respectively, while Green-LLM [39] optimizes request flows
with a linear program. FREESH [40] periodically provisions
inference workers across DCs based on marginal emissions
and load, scaling GPU frequency to meet its latency targets.
GCOS [41] migrates GPU jobs across DCs using multi-agent
reinforcement learning. Only MOER [43] operates at per-
request scheduling granularity using marginal CI signals. As
discussed in Section I, these works rely on coarse-grained
decisions and batch-agnostic latency and power models without
engine queueing. Meanwhile, LLM serving simulators such
as Vidur [83] and LLMServingSim [84], [85] model various
inference features within a single cluster, including batching,
routing, disaggregated serving, KV-cache offloading, and prefix
caching, yet none capture batch-dependent power, inter-DC
transfers, or carbon across multiple DCs. To our knowledge,
ours is the first study that jointly models continuous batching,
engine queueing, inter-DC transfers, and per-DC power and
carbon with hardware-calibrated latency and power models
at geo-distributed scale, and evaluates carbon savings against
per-token SLO attainment across various models on MLPerf
benchmarks and SLOs.
VIII. CONCLUSION
In this work, we present a geo-distributed LLM inference
simulator, calibrated against real hardware, that models continu-
ous batching, engine queueing, inter-DC transfers, and per-DC
power and carbon. Further, we use the proposed simulator to
map the carbon–SLO frontier of greedy, ILP-, and MILP-based
schedulers across three models and load regimes under MLPerf
SLOs. The facility MILP scheduler, which captures both batch-
dependent carbon and latency within a scheduling window,
offers the best carbon–SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions
from 26% to 60% across varying loads compared to the RR
policy, with an average SLO violation of 3%. We observe that
(i) the carbon savings grow with the CI spread across DCs and
shrink with the load, (ii) the topology trades them against SLO
violations, and (iii) SLO attainment depends on the load-update
frequency. We further reveal that our findings hold under real
PUE values and predicted OSLs, thereby strengthening their
applicability to practical deployments. These results suggest
that accounting for batch-dependent latency and power allows
schedulers to reduce carbon while largely meeting per-token
SLOs. As future work, we plan to extend the study to multi-
turn sessions, where KV-cache locality couples consecutive
10


--- Page 11 ---
placements, and to heterogeneous inference scenarios with
varying models and deployment configurations across DCs.
ACKNOWLEDGMENT
We used Claude (Anthropic) [86] as an assistant for text
revision, grammar checking, and code development of the
simulator and analysis scripts. The research ideas, system and
scheduler designs, experiments, and conclusions are the authors’
own, and the authors verified all AI-assisted content.
